title: Dw i'n … / Wyt ti'n …?
why: Say what you do: Dw i'n dysgu Cymraeg. Ask: Wyt ti'n siarad Cymraeg?

grammar.explain: To say what you do, use "Dw i'n" + verb: Dw i'n dysgu = I learn / I'm learning. To ask someone, use "Wyt ti'n" + verb? To answer yes or no, Welsh usually echoes the verb: "Ydw" (yes, I do / I am) or "Nac ydw" (no, I don't / I'm not). For not, say "Dw i ddim yn" + verb.

title: Ydw / Nac ydw · Dw i ddim yn …
why: Answer yes/no questions and say what you don’t do.

grammar.explain: Welsh has no single word for 'yes' or 'no'. You echo the verb. To 'Wyt ti'n…?' answer Ydw (yes, I am/do) or Nac ydw (no). To 'Ydy hi/o…?' answer Ydy or Nac ydy. To say what you don't do: Dw i ddim yn + verb. Describing words after yn take soft mutation: cyffrous → gyffrous, trist → drist.

title: Mae'n braf: describing with yn + soft mutation

title: Fy / dy / ei: my, your, his/her (with mutations)
why: Talk about your family: fy nhad, dy fam, ei chwaer.

grammar.explain: Each 'my/your/his/her' word changes the next word. Fy (my) adds a nasal mutation: tad → fy nhad, brawd → fy mrawd. Dy (your) adds soft mutation: mam → dy fam. Ei (his) adds soft mutation: ei dad o. Ei (her) adds aspirate: tad → ei thad hi, and an h before vowels: ei henw hi. Speakers often add i/o/hi after the noun.

why: Compare: Mae te yn well na coffi. Y lle gorau.

grammar.explain: To compare, say 'yn fwy na' (bigger/more than) or 'yn well na' (better than). After 'yn', adjectives take soft mutation: 'mwy' becomes 'fwy' and 'gwell' becomes 'well'. title: Dw i ddim yn gwybod os / be / lle …
why: Indirect questions: Dw i ddim yn siŵr lle mae o.

grammar.explain: To say what you don't know, start with 'Dw i ddim yn gwybod' or 'Dw i ddim yn siŵr', then add pwy (who), be (what), lle (where), pryd (when) or os (if). After os, use 'ydy' (os ydy o'n hen). Also use 'ydy' after pwy or be when you ask who or what something is (pwy ydy hwn, be ydy hwnna). After lle and pryd, and after be when an action follows, use 'mae' (lle mae o, be mae o isio). For the past, use 'roedd' (lle roedd y teulu'n byw). The rest of the sentence stays just like a normal statement.

title: Cymraeg y Wladfa: Spanish words and local ways
why: Recognise Patagonian Welsh: Spanish loans, greetings, places.

grammar.explain: Welsh in Y Wladfa borrows Spanish words freely. Small words like che (hey/mate), bueno, claro and chau drop straight into Welsh sentences. Spanish nouns stay as they are: y colectivo (the bus), y kiosco. Borrowed verbs get the Welsh ending -io, so they work like any Welsh verb: retirio (to retire), just like clicio. Listen for them: they're a sign you're in Patagonia!

title: On camera: street-interview questions
why: The questions you’ll ask on camera, and how to react.

grammar.explain: Street-interview questions are short. 'Dach chi'n...?' = Do you...? 'Be ydy...?' = What is...? 'Be dach chi'n licio am...?' = What do you like about...? After 'am' you get soft mutation: Cymru → Gymru. React fast with: 'Wir?' (Really?), 'Bobol bach!' (Goodness!), 'Yn hollol!' (Exactly!), 'Diolch yn fawr iawn!'

title: The final: introduce yourself and interview someone
why: Five minutes of Welsh, start to finish.

grammar.explain: Today you put it all together. Start with yourself: 'Fy enw i ydy...', 'Dw i'n...'. Then ask: 'Ga i ofyn cwestiwn i chi?', 'Sgynnoch chi...?' (do you have...?), 'Ers pryd dach chi'n...?'. 'Sgynnoch chi' and 'sgen i' are the spoken northern forms of 'oes gynnoch chi' and 'oes gen i'. So 'Sgen i ddim...' means the same as 'Does gen i ddim...' (I haven't got...). The thing you have takes a soft mutation: plant → blant.
